title: Lattice quantum electrodynamics of a molecular emitter in a topological gap
authors: Clarisse Fournier, Johannes Düreth, Elena Fanella, Hugo Levy-Falk, Maja Colautti, Anna Beauvironnet, Gauthier Dekyndt, Clément Hainaut, Tomáš Neuman, Simon Betzold, Sven Höfling, Sebastian Klembt, Alejandro González-Tudela, Costanza Toninelli, Alberto Amo
abstract: Engineering the photonic environment using lattices of coupled resonators, which we refer to as lattice quantum electrodynamics (QED), provides a route to control both the spontaneous emission of individual quantum emitters and the photon-mediated interactions between them. Here we introduce an optical lattice QED platform based on individual dibenzoterrylene (DBT) molecules embedded in anthracene crystals and coupled to lattices of open optical microcavities. This hybrid architecture benefits from narrow-linewidth molecular emitters, site-resolved optical access, engineered coupled-resonator bands, and compatibility with established molecular frequency-tuning techniques. As a proof-of-principle demonstration, we observe emitter-photon bound states formed when the optical transition of a single molecule is tuned to the band gap of a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) cavity lattice. These in-gap states display directional localization and photon emission on a single sublattice, inherited from the vacancy-induced topological edge modes of the underlying SSH lattice. Our results establish open-cavity lattices coupled to DBT molecules as a versatile architecture for engineering many-emitter quantum optical systems with controllable photon-mediated interactions.
summary: The paper introduces an optical lattice Quantum Electrodynamics platform using embedded organic molecules coupled to structured microcavities. By tuning the molecular emission into the photonic band gap of a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) lattice, the researchers successfully observed topological edge mode characteristics in emitter-photon bound states. This establishes a versatile architecture for engineering complex quantum optical systems with controlled interactions.
main_problem: The research aims to control both the spontaneous emission of individual quantum emitters and the photon-mediated interactions between them by engineering the photonic environment.
main_result: The authors demonstrated emitter-photon bound states exhibiting directional localization on a single sublattice when the molecule's transition is tuned into the topological band gap of an SSH cavity lattice.
method: The study uses a hybrid platform combining molecular emitters (DBT) embedded in crystals with engineered optical microcavity lattices to realize controlled light-matter coupling.
model_or_system: The system utilizes open optical cavities structured into lattices, specifically demonstrating behavior analogous to Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chains. The physics is modeled using cavity QED principles applied to coupled resonators.
key_observables: Emitter-photon bound states, directional photon emission on a single sublattice, and the characterization of photonic band gaps.
important_parameters: The system operates at specific wavelengths (e.g., 782 nm) and involves tuning the molecular transition relative to the engineered photonic band structure ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The architecture assumes that coupling to engineered band structures allows for precise control over interactions, extending beyond single-molecule demonstrations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical setup (open cavity sketch, optical images) and show photoluminescence spectra demonstrating spectral dependence on detuning ($\Delta$) within the lattice structure.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general concept of Lattice QED to detailing the specific hybrid architecture using DBT molecules. It then presents proof-of-principle measurements by observing topological edge mode characteristics in bound states formed within a cavity SSH lattice.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it combines molecular physics (DBT emitters) with advanced concepts from condensed matter theory, specifically topological photonics and engineered band structures, to create a controllable quantum light-matter interface.
